title: Why Weather Is Getting Wilder
summary:
Have you noticed more crazy weather lately? Scientists say it's because of climate change—when the Earth gets warmer because of gases like carbon dioxide. These gases come from burning coal, gas, and oil.

A long time ago, in the 1850s, a scientist named Eunice Newton Foote did an experiment. She put carbon dioxide in glass jars and left them in the sun. They got hotter than jars with other stuff. That was a clue!

Now, the Earth is 1.44 degrees Celsius warmer than in the 1800s. That might not sound like much, but it makes weather more extreme. We're seeing bigger wildfires, like Australia's 'Black Summer' in 2019-2020, when 19 million hectares burned. And floods, like in Pakistan in 2022, when a third of the country was under water.

Some scientists are worried. Daniel Swain says it's like the 'Boy Who Cried Wolf'—people might not believe them, but the danger is real. Another scientist, Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, says even if we stop adding greenhouse gases, the damage will last for centuries. She compares it to a frog in boiling water—if the water heats slowly, the frog doesn't notice.

But there's hope. We can reduce emissions and prepare for extreme weather. It's up to us to pay attention and take action. What do you think we should do?
why_it_matters: Understanding climate change helps you see why weather is getting wilder and why small actions to save energy can make a difference for the planet you will grow up on.

background_read: Scientists have known for a long time that some gases trap heat.
Eunice Newton Foote (a scientist who ran an early experiment with carbon dioxide in the 1850s) was one of the first to show this.
Today, researchers like Daniel Swain and Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick (climate scientists who study extreme weather) warn that warming can make wildfires and floods worse.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists like Eunice Newton Foote, Daniel Swain, and Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick studied climate change and extreme weather.
WHAT: The Earth has warmed by 1.44 degrees Celsius since the 1800s, causing wilder weather like bigger wildfires and floods.
WHERE: Around the world, including Australia's 'Black Summer' wildfires and Pakistan's 2022 floods.
WHY: Burning coal, gas, and oil puts carbon dioxide and greenhouse gases into the air, and the damage can last for centuries.

perspectives.description: Some scientists worry people won't believe warnings, like the Boy Who Cried Wolf, even though the danger is real.
The article says there is hope because we can reduce emissions and prepare for extreme weather.
Communities in Australia and Pakistan have already seen huge wildfires and floods, so paying attention to climate change matters.
